source: derived from the clause 3 P-field and T-field layouts
note: Time code P-field and T-field wire layouts. Scope note: these vectors pin the packing only, from explicit field values. They do not cover conversion from a civil timestamp, because Level 1 CUC applies a TAI-UTC offset from a leap-second table, and pinning octets through that path would fix the table rather than the standard's layout. See COVERAGE.md.

encode.name: pfield-cuc-level-1-no-extension
encode.note: The P-field is one octet: bit 7 is the extension flag, bits 6-4 the time code identification, bits 3-0 format-specific detail. Extension clear, time code ID 1, detail 0 gives 0<<7 | 1<<4 | 0 = 0x10.

encode.name: pfield-detail-all-ones
encode.note: The same P-field with all four detail bits set: 1<<4 | 0xf = 0x1f. Pins that detail occupies the low nibble and does not bleed into the time code ID.

encode.name: pfield-with-extension-flag
encode.note: Extension set, time code ID 2, detail 4: octet 0 = 1<<7 | 2<<4 | 4 = 0xa4. The extension flag means a second P-field octet follows, so the field is two octets and the second carries the 7-bit extension detail — here zero. The flag and the octet count cannot disagree: a one-octet field with the flag set is not representable.

encode.name: cuc-tfield-coarse-one-second
encode.note: CUC T-field with 4 coarse octets and no fine octets: coarse time 1 second since the epoch, big-endian, gives 00 00 00 01.

encode.name: cuc-tfield-coarse-distinct-octets
encode.note: Coarse time 0x12345678 with 4 octets: every octet differs, so a byte-order error shows up immediately as 78563412.

encode.name: cuc-tfield-with-one-fine-octet
encode.note: Coarse 1 with a single fine octet 0x80, which is one half-second at that resolution: 00 00 00 01 80. The fine octets follow the coarse ones, most significant first.

encode.name: cuc-tfield-coarse-maximum
encode.note: All four coarse octets set: ff ff ff ff, about 136 years of seconds. Pins the field width.

encode.name: cds-tfield-day-one
encode.note: CDS T-field with a 16-bit day segment and no sub-millisecond octets: day 1, zero milliseconds of day, giving 00 01 followed by the 4-octet millisecond count 00 00 00 00.

encode.name: cds-tfield-last-millisecond-of-the-day
encode.note: Day 0x1234 with 86399999 milliseconds, the last millisecond before midnight: 12 34 then 0x05265bff. A decoder that allowed 86400000 would be accepting a time that does not exist.

encode.name: cds-tfield-24-bit-day-with-submilliseconds
encode.note: The wide form: a 24-bit day segment and two sub-millisecond octets. Day 1, 1 millisecond, sub-millisecond 2, giving 00 00 01 then 00 00 00 01 then 00 02.

encode.name: pfield-extension-detail-bits
encode.note: The same extended P-field with all seven extension detail bits set: octet 1 = 0x7f. Bit 0 of the second octet is itself reserved by CCSDS 301.0-B-4 for a third octet that the standard never defines, so 0x7f is the largest legal value and 0xff must be refused — see the pfield-further-extension-bit-set reject vector.

reject.name: cuc-shorter-than-a-pfield-and-tfield
reject.note: A CUC needs at least a P-field octet and one T-field octet.

reject.name: cuc-tfield-shorter-than-the-pfield-declares
reject.note: The P-field says four coarse octets follow but only two do. A decoder must refuse rather than read past the buffer or zero-extend.

reject.name: pfield-further-extension-bit-set
reject.note: Bit 0 of the second P-field octet is reserved for a third octet the standard does not define. A set bit must be refused rather than silently misparsing the next octet as T-field data, which would shift every time value that followed.
